title: GRC-2025-CM-0132
description: This is a conceptual video produced with the goal of showing external agencies what their future firefighting operations could be like if NASA develops this software.  The Common Operating Picture (or COP) supplies everyone involved with the same information and utilizes AI technology to quickly obtain 3D topo maps, fire spread predictions, weather from satellites and ground bases, entry and exit routes, and available personnel and equipment. The dispatcher and incident commander need this RF communication to make important decisions.  Feedback on its feasibility is requested by first responders for development and implementation.

transcript.text: The following story is fictional.
Its intent is to portray a future
wildland firefighting system that uses AI
trained in wildland firefighting and fast response
drones to augment the skills of humans and the equipment
and tactics currently in use.
Please send your comments to david.folaratnasa.gov.
A July morning in Colorado's White River National Forest,
Don's Hot and Dry.
At 0847 Mountain, a ghost satellite
detects a heat signature in the area.
Within seconds, the data reaches the US Forest Service's
regional operations center, where the Fire Responder AI
system flags it as a wildland fire ignition.
The nearest quick response drone
is an Eagle County Regional Airport's Fire Operations
hangar.
The system dispatches a drone, equipped with its own AI,
specifically trained to perform the initial size up.
It has the latest topo maps on board,
along with current and forecasted weather and current moisture
density in the area.
At the same time, USFS Ranger David Fuller
receives the alert on his tablet
and begins driving to the nearest access point,
an hour's hike from the suspected fire.
The Fire Responder AI system shows him the best route
to get there.
On route, the drone creates a communications link
to the ground station at Eagle County Airport.
This network will become the local tactical network used
by all parties for the common operating picture, or COP.
Maintaining situation awareness for the response team.
By 0900, the drone arrives on scene
and begins to orbit the fire.
Its thermal camera maps the fire's perimeter,
while the AI system processes data from nearby remote automated
weather stations, 92 degrees Fahrenheit,
12% moisture density, and 15 to 20 mile per hour wind gusts
through dead standing trees.
The drone AI begins evaluating threats, escape routes,
safety zones, and ingress egress vulnerabilities
for ground assets.
This information is uploaded to the Denver Dispat Center
and incorporated into the COP virtual space.
The COP is made available to all assets
assigned to the incident.
At the Dispat Center, incident commander Maria Rodriguez
monitors the emerging situation.
The Denver AI merges the drone's live data of the fire sprint
and displays on Maria's monitor its predicted advance
of a steep gunch filled with a dead standing temporary.
She accesses a resource dashboard.
The AI also displays all available resources.
Three type one helicopters at nearby bases.
Two air tankers working a Wyoming fire
but available for diversion.
And more hot shot crews within two hours drive time.
Maria recognizes the need for air support
and assigns an air tactical crew supervisor, or ATGS,
to coordinate flies into the fire zone.
She selects the air resources and the AI
notifies them to launch.
The drone circles overhead, maintaining the network
for the emerging response.
At 0945, the first engines and crews arrive.
Their mobile devices automatically joining the network.
Each device displays the COP, fire locations,
spread prediction, escape routes, and safety zones.
The ATGS arrives on scene and begins orbiting the fire.
Their workstation automatically joins the network
and exchanges information with the incident commander
and ground teams.
On the ATGS workstation is a list of incoming assets,
their status and ETA.
The ATGS begins coordinating with the ground teams.
The ground crew chiefs use their handheld tablets
to mark where drops are needed.
Share this information with the ATGS over the network
and confirm by voice.
The ATGS assigns targets to the air tankers via the network.
Flight paths to targets, drop points,
and locations of nearby ground teams
are then sent to the air tankers,
where the pilots can see the information
in their head of display.
Drones and AI technology trained in wildland firefighting
can monitor many data streams and flag
increasing risk indicators.
These decision support tools can help wildland firefighters
make safe, effective decisions quickly.
Drones and AI, utilizing a local tactical network,
can share this information to the entire response team,
building and maintaining the common operating picture
in real time.
As aerial and ground assets enter the area,
they automatically join the network.
Their ID, position, intent, capabilities, and resources
are integrated into the COP and made available to all responders.
The ATGS, coordinating with the IC and ground teams,
can designate drop points, which are shared in the COP.
The air tanker pilots see approach routes
and drop points in their HUD.
This future concept of operations can become reality,
with NASA's advanced capabilities
for emergency response operations projects.
A Sarrow.

pass_reason: Conceptual dramatization, not a real event
